title: Static members
summary: Know what belongs to each object and what belongs to the type itself.

steps.title: One per object, or one for the whole class
body: Everything you have put in a class so far is an **instance** member: each object gets its own copy.
A **static** member belongs to the class itself. There is exactly one, however many objects exist, even if none do.
```csharp
var a = new Ticket();
var b = new Ticket();
Console.WriteLine(b.Number);        // 2
Console.WriteLine(Ticket.Issued);   // 2
class Ticket
public static int Issued;      // one, shared by all tickets
public int Number { get; }     // one per ticket
public Ticket()
Issued++;
Number = Issued;
You reach a static member through the **class name**: `Ticket.Issued`. You reach an instance member through an **object**: `b.Number`.
You have used statics since day one. `Console.WriteLine`, `Math.Max` and `int.Parse` are all called on a type, not on an object.

steps.prompt: Which values are shared and which are per parcel? What does this print?
steps.explain: `Count` and `TotalWeight` are static, so all three constructors update the same two variables. `Weight` is per object.

steps.prompt: Given this `Ticket` class and `var a = new Ticket();`, which line compiles?
steps.explain: Static members are reached through the class name. `Ticket.Number` fails because `Number` needs a particular ticket: which one would it be?

steps.title: Static methods and static classes
body: A method can be static too. It has no object to work on, so it can only use its parameters and other static members.
Some classes are nothing but static helpers. Mark the whole class `static` and the compiler guarantees nobody can `new` it.
```csharp
Console.WriteLine(Vat.AddTo(100m));   // 120.00
static class Vat
public static decimal AddTo(decimal net)
return net * 1.20m;
A static class is the right home for **pure helpers**: methods where the answer depends only on the arguments. Same input, same output, nothing remembered. `Math` is the classic example.
> **Tip:** Inside a static method, using an instance field is a compile error. There is no *this object* to read it from.

steps.prompt: Is each call made on a type (static) or on an object (instance)?
steps.explain: Look at what is left of the dot. A type name means static. A variable holding an object means instance.

steps.title: A static greeter
prompt: Write a **static class** `Greeter`. Your `Sk.GreetingFor(hour, day)` from Control flow is ready to call (it returns `"Good morning"`, `"Enjoy your weekend"` and so on).
- `static string Hello(string name, int hour, DayOfWeek day)` returns `"<greeting>, <name>. Sidekick is ready."`, built from `Sk.GreetingFor` and `AppName`.
`Greeter.Hello("Ada", 9, DayOfWeek.Monday)` returns `"Good morning, Ada. Sidekick is ready."`.
solution: public static string Hello(string name, int hour, DayOfWeek day)
template: Dojo.Eq("Monday morning", "Good morning, Ada. Sidekick is ready.", Greeter.Hello("Ada", 9, DayOfWeek.Monday));
Dojo.Eq("Tuesday evening", "Good evening, Ada. Sidekick is ready.", Greeter.Hello("Ada", 20, DayOfWeek.Tuesday));
Dojo.Eq("Saturday", "Slow weekend morning, Sam. Sidekick is ready.", Greeter.Hello("Sam", 10, DayOfWeek.Saturday));
Dojo.Check("AppName is a const", typeof(Greeter).GetField("AppName")?.IsLiteral == true, "declare it with const");
Dojo.Check("Greeter is a static class", typeof(Greeter).IsAbstract && typeof(Greeter).IsSealed, "write static class Greeter");
internal static string GreetingFor(int hour, DayOfWeek day)
bool weekend = day == DayOfWeek.Saturday || day == DayOfWeek.Sunday;
result = hour < 12 ? "Slow weekend morning" : "Enjoy your weekend";
hints: `public static string Hello(...) => $"{Sk.GreetingFor(hour, day)}, {name}. {AppName} is ready.";`

steps.title: const and readonly
body: Two ways to say *this never changes*:
```csharp
class Invoice
public const decimal VatRate = 0.20m;   // fixed when the code is compiled
private static int _nextNumber = 1;     // shared, and it changes
public readonly int Number;             // set once per invoice
public Invoice()
Number = _nextNumber;
_nextNumber++;
- `const` is a value known **before the program runs**. It works for numbers, strings and `bool`. It is automatically shared by the whole class, so you write `Invoice.VatRate`.
- `readonly` is set **while the program runs**, in the constructor, and locked afterwards. Each object can have a different value.
- `static readonly` is one shared value that is set once at startup. Use it for things `const` cannot hold, such as a list.
Why bother? A named constant explains itself. `price * 0.20m` makes the reader guess. `price * Invoice.VatRate` does not, and when the rate changes there is one place to edit.

steps.prompt: Match each declaration to how its value behaves.
pairs: fixed at compile time, the same for everyone
set once per object, in the constructor
one shared value that can keep changing
one per object, and it can keep changing
one shared value, set once when the program starts

steps.prompt: `MaxWeightKg` is a fixed rule known when the code is compiled. `_created` counts every shipment ever made. `TrackingCode` is set once per shipment and never changes.
steps.explain: A compile-time rule is `const`. A shared counter that changes is `static`. A per-object value locked after construction is `readonly`.

steps.title: When static is a smell
body: Static is tempting because it is reachable from everywhere. That is also the danger.
```csharp
static class CurrentCart
public static List<string> Items = new List<string>();
public static decimal Total;

This is a **global variable** wearing a class. Any line of code anywhere can change it, so when the total is wrong you have the whole program to search. There can only ever be one cart, so two customers at once is impossible. And a test cannot start with a fresh cart, because the old values are still there.
A rule of thumb:
- **Good static:** constants, and pure helpers that remember nothing (`Math.Round`, `Vat.AddTo`).
- **Suspicious static:** anything that holds data which changes while the program runs.
If it has state that changes, it probably wants to be an object you create and pass to whoever needs it.

steps.prompt: Which of these are **good** uses of `static`? Select all that apply.
options: A static field holding the logged-in user's shopping cart
A static `decimal Balance` on `BankAccount` so every method can reach it
steps.explain: The first two never change and remember nothing. The other two are shared, changing state: every account would have the same balance, and every user the same cart.

steps.title: Sidekick piece: task codes
prompt: **Sidekick piece.** Every task has a short code: `SK-007`. You type it (`sk done SK-007`, or just `sk done 7`), Sidekick prints it in every list. One static class owns the rule.
- `static string Format(int id)`: the prefix and the id with at least three digits (`{id:000}`): `7` gives `"SK-007"`, `1234` gives `"SK-1234"`;
- `static bool TryParse(string text, out int id)`: reads `"SK-007"` (any case), `"#7"` or `"7"`, with spaces around allowed. `true` only when what is left is a whole number of 1 or more;
- `static int Next(IEnumerable<int> used)`: one more than the largest id in `used`, or 1 when there are none.
solution: public static bool TryParse(string text, out int id)
template: Dojo.Check("Prefix is a const", typeof(Ids).GetField("Prefix")?.IsLiteral == true, "declare it with const");
Dojo.Check("Ids is a static class", typeof(Ids).IsAbstract && typeof(Ids).IsSealed, "write static class Ids");
Dojo.Eq("Next of nothing is 1", 1, Ids.Next(new int[0]));
Dojo.Eq("Next of a list", 11, Ids.Next(new List<int> { 10 }));
(bool, int) dojoParse(string s) { bool ok = Ids.TryParse(s, out int id); return (ok, id); }
hints: `TryParse`: trim, then cut the prefix off with `Substring(Prefix.Length)` when `StartsWith(Prefix, StringComparison.OrdinalIgnoreCase)`, or a leading `#`.
End with `return int.TryParse(t, out id) && id > 0;`. `Next` keeps the largest id seen, starting from 0, and adds 1.
steps.explain: Nothing here belongs to one task: the prefix and the rules are the same for all of them, so they live on the type, as `static` members and a `const`.
